q: Percentages for each grape run along the foot of a back label whose front names no grape at all. What obliges the producer to print them?
opts: Nothing; a breakdown of a blend is voluntary
It is required whenever no single grape reaches half of the wine
It is required for wines sold above a set price
European law requires it for any wine that is a blend
exp: Producers print a breakdown because it interests the kind of buyer who reads back labels, not because anyone made them do it. The proportions can shift from vintage to vintage while the front label stays exactly as it was, which is one reason many producers would rather not commit to figures at all. What is compulsory on a label sits elsewhere, and the make-up of a blend is not part of it.

q: A European label naming two grapes rather than one makes a promise that a single name does not. What is it?
opts: That the two were fermented together rather than blended afterwards
That the wine is made entirely from the two varieties named
That the wine was aged in oak before bottling
That the two came from separate vineyards
exp: Naming one variety leaves a margin behind it that need not be declared anywhere; naming two closes that margin, because the pair have to account for the whole wine. A producer with a small third component therefore either leaves it out of the blend or leaves the second name off the label. A wine that cannot make the promise simply names one grape, or none.

q: Six varieties go into a blend and not one of them dominates it, so the front of the bottle carries an invented name instead. What lies behind that choice?
opts: No one grape carries enough of the wine to be named alone, and six names sell nothing
Blends of more than three varieties may not be sold under any name
An invented name is required whenever the fruit comes from several vineyards
A producer must invent a name once the wine is exported
exp: A label may name one grape by itself only where that grape carries the wine, and a genuinely equal blend has no such grape. Naming every variety in the blend is the lawful alternative, and six names across a front label sell nothing, so the producer builds a name of his own and then spends years teaching buyers what stands behind it. Several of the most admired wines in the world are sold exactly that way, so an invented name is no evidence of a modest bottle.

q: A Californian back label calls the wine a Bordeaux blend, and not a drop of French wine is in it. What is that phrase claiming?
opts: That the winemaker trained in Bordeaux
That the wine may lawfully use the region's name
That part of the fruit was bought in from Bordeaux
The set of grape varieties used, and nothing more
exp: Phrases of this kind borrow a region's name as shorthand for a recipe, say nothing whatever about where the fruit grew, and carry no legal weight anywhere. They are useful to a buyer all the same, since they say in two words what a list of varieties takes a line to say. In Europe such wording runs straight into the protection given to the region's name, which is why it is far commoner on labels written for other markets.

q: An estate sells its single varieties cheaply and reserves a blend for its most expensive bottling. What does that arrangement say about blending?
opts: That blends are cheaper to produce than single varieties
That a blend is required at the top of any range
That the estate's varietal wines failed to qualify for their appellation
That blending is a tool for building a better wine, not a sign of a lesser one
exp: Varieties ripen at different moments and cover each other's weaknesses from one year to the next, so a blend can be both more consistent and more complete than any of its parts. The idea that blending hides something comes from the cheapest end of the trade, where it often does. Most of the classic wines of Europe are blends and most of them never say so on the label.

q: A pink wine names a black grape on its front label and a guest calls it an error. What should you tell them?
opts: The colour came from the barrel, so no grape name applies
The label is right, since a rose is made from black grapes given only brief skin contact
The label should name the white grape that the wine was blended with
The label names the grape the vineyard is planted to rather than the one in the wine
exp: Colour sits in the skins and not in the juice, so the same black grape gives a red wine, a pink one or a white one depending on how long the two are left together. A varietal rose is therefore named after a black grape as a matter of course. It is among the most common questions asked at a table in summer and among the easiest to answer well.

q: Four labels from four countries open a grape's name with Tinta, Tinto, Nero and Blau. What do those four words announce?
opts: That the grape is a mutation of a white variety
That the grape is black-skinned
That the wine will be dry
That the wine was matured in wood
exp: Colour words are among the most dependable things in grape naming: the Iberian pair, the Italian word and the German one all mark a dark-skinned vine. It is the quickest way into an unfamiliar name on a label in a language you cannot read. Nothing in the word promises a style, and vines of this kind turn out everything from the palest pink to the blackest red in the country.

q: A southern French white is labelled Grenache Blanc and a red beside it is labelled Grenache. What does that extra word mark?
opts: A blend of the black grape with a white one
A white wine pressed quickly from the black grape, before it colours
A white-berried mutation of the same vine, bottled on its own
A younger selection of the same variety
exp: Vines throw colour mutations often enough that several familiar varieties exist in more than one colour, each with a settled name and a settled character of its own. This one is fuller and lower in acid than its black counterpart and is a mainstay of the white blends of the Mediterranean south. A pale wine pressed from a black grape is a different thing entirely and has its own vocabulary.

q: A Sicilian red is labelled Nero d'Avola and a guest takes Avola for the appellation. What is that word doing in the name?
opts: It names the appellation the wine comes from, which is why the two run together
It belongs to the variety's name, recording a town the grape is tied to
It marks a superior selection of the variety
It names the estate that grew the fruit
exp: Grape names built out of a place are common, and the place inside them is a piece of history rather than an origin claim, since the vine can be planted anywhere that suits it. The appellation, where there is one, is stated separately and in its own form of words. Reading the two as one line is among the easiest mistakes to make on an Italian label.

q: Two bottles of Chardonnay from opposite ends of the world taste nothing alike, and a guest asks whether one of them has been mislabelled. What is the answer?
opts: The difference means that one of the two wines is faulty
One of them must have been made from a different variety
Neither has; a variety name promises the grape, never a style
The riper of the two must have had another grape blended into it
exp: Climate, yield, picking date, vessel and the winemaker's intention move a wine much further than identity does, which is how one grape arrives lean and stony in one glass and broad and buttery in the next. A variety name opens a conversation rather than describing a taste. Saying what that grape usually does in that particular place is the useful half of the answer.

q: A guest asks for the grape they drank on holiday in Spain and nothing on your list carries that name. What is the first thing to check?
opts: Whether the guest has remembered the name correctly
Whether the list already holds the same variety under another country's name for it
Whether something similar can be poured without mentioning the substitution
Whether a case can be ordered in for that evening
exp: A great many varieties sit on a list twice under two names, and a sommelier who knows the synonyms says yes where a colleague says no. It is the most practical everyday use of synonym knowledge there is. Naming the alternative openly also leaves the guest with something they will use again.

q: A guest who has enjoyed a bottle wants the grape written down so they can buy it at home, and the vine travels under a different name where they live. Which name goes on the card?
opts: The name vine scientists use in their catalogues, since that is the one form recognised everywhere
The name on the bottle in front of them, since a variety may only be sold under the name its producer chose
The name printed where the guest shops, since that is the form their own shelf will carry
The name used where the vine originated, since every other country's register is built from that form
exp: The same vine reaches shelves under one name in one market and another name somewhere else, so the useful name is whichever one the guest's own shop prints. Vine scientists do settle on a reference name for their catalogues, and it carries no authority over a label and will never appear above a shop shelf. A recommendation the guest cannot act on when they get home has not really been given.

q: Divers working a Roman wreck bring up hundreds of tall clay jars with pointed bases, sealed at the neck with pitch and stamped with a maker's mark. What are these wine containers called?
opts: Wineskins
Amphorae
Puncheons
Demijohns
exp: The pointed base let a jar be stood upright in sand or stacked in a ship's hold, and the pitch lining sealed clay that would otherwise have leaked. The stamps on the handles and rims are how the ancient wine trade is traced today, since a jar found in Britain can be matched to the kiln that made it.

q: Seafaring merchants out of the Levantine coast carried vine cuttings west to Carthage, Sicily and the coast of Iberia long before Rome had a fleet of its own. Which people were they?
opts: The Etruscans
The Vandals
The Normans
The Phoenicians
exp: Their trading posts around the western Mediterranean give the first evidence of vines in several countries that now build whole economies on wine. Greek colonists followed and planted the south of Italy so thoroughly that it was known to the ancient world as the land of vines.

q: Roman traders working north of the Alps found the tribes there using a container of bent staves and hoops, lighter than clay and far harder to break on a cart. Who is credited with the wooden barrel?
opts: The Celtic peoples of Gaul
The Norse
The Egyptians of the Nile delta
Greek colonists in southern Italy
exp: Wood could be rolled by one man, repaired, and refilled for years, and it survived roads that would have destroyed a cargo of jars. Rome adopted it for bulk movement across the western provinces, and the trade has used a hooped wooden vessel ever since.

q: An emperor ordered provincial vineyards cut back in AD 92, wanting grain planted in their place and provincial wine kept away from Rome's own market. Which emperor?
opts: Constantine
Domitian
Nero
Augustus
exp: The edict is usually read as protection for Italian growers dressed up as a grain policy, and it was widely ignored outside Italy. Probus is credited with lifting the restriction nearly two centuries later, after which planting in Gaul, Spain and the Rhineland expanded without hindrance.
